## Introduction

The `ospsuite.parameteridentification` package provides tools to estimate model parameters by fitting simulations to observed data. After the optimization step, confidence intervals (CIs) can be used to assess the uncertainty of the estimated parameters and to evaluate how robust the results are.

This vignette describes the available methods for confidence interval estimation, explains how to configure and run them, and shows how to inspect the results.

The examples use `piTask`, a `ParameterIdentification` object, and `outputMapping`, one of its `PIOutputMapping` objects, created as shown in the [user guide](user-guide.html).

## Choosing a CI Method

-   **`hessian`** is the default method. It estimates confidence intervals from the curvature of the objective function at the optimum. This approach is fast and works well when the problem is well-behaved and the objective function is approximately quadratic.

-   **`PL`** (profile likelihood) computes confidence intervals by scanning the likelihood along each parameter. It is more robust for parameters near bounds or in situations where the likelihood is not well approximated by a quadratic shape, but it is slower.

-   **`bootstrap`** generates confidence intervals by repeatedly refitting the model to new versions of the observed data. It makes no assumption about the shape of the likelihood, but it assumes that the individual data sets are exchangeable and, for aggregated data, that the means follow a lognormal distribution with the spread given by the reported SD and the number of subjects. It is computationally more intensive than the other methods. The section [Bootstrap Resampling](#bootstrap-resampling) describes how the data are resampled.

## Configuring CI Estimation

Each confidence interval method provides a predefined set of default options. These defaults are available through the helper objects `CIOptions_hessian`, `CIOptions_PL`, and `CIOptions_bootstrap`. The corresponding object is assigned to `piConfiguration$ciOptions` and individual fields can then be modified as required.

### Options

Common options:

- `confLevel`: confidence level (e.g. `0.95` for 95% confidence intervals)

Additional options for the Hessian method:

- `epsilon`: step size of the numerical derivatives
- `r`, `d`: settings of the Richardson extrapolation in `numDeriv::hessian()`

Additional options for profile likelihood (PL):

- `epsilon`: step size of the profile
- `maxIter`: maximum number of iterations

Additional options for bootstrap:

- `nBootstrap`: number of bootstrap resamples
- `seed`: random seed for reproducibility

If no method is specified, the default is the **`hessian`** method with its standard options.

### Example

Configuration of confidence intervals is done through the `PIConfiguration` object, which also holds all other settings for parameter identification. The example below shows how the Hessian method is selected and its default options adjusted:

```{r}
piConfiguration <- PIConfiguration$new()

# select CI method
piConfiguration$ciMethod <- "hessian"

# assign default options and adjust if necessary
piConfiguration$ciOptions <- CIOptions_hessian
piConfiguration$ciOptions$confLevel <- 0.95
```

### Running CI Estimation Separately

By default, confidence intervals are estimated immediately after each optimization run (`autoEstimateCI = TRUE`). To disable this behaviour and perform CI estimation later, set the flag to `FALSE`:

```{r}
piConfiguration$autoEstimateCI <- FALSE
```

In this case, the optimization is executed first and CI estimation is triggered explicitly when needed, for example to review results before running the more time-consuming CI calculation.

```{r}
piResult <- piTask$run()
piResult <- piTask$estimateCI()
```

## Bootstrap Resampling

Each bootstrap replicate builds a new version of the observed data and fits the model to it again. The spread of the estimates across the replicates gives the confidence interval. How a replicate is built depends on the kind of observed data, and one task can contain both kinds.

### Individual Data

Data sets with individual values, for example one data set per subject, are drawn with replacement within each output mapping. A data set drawn twice counts twice in the fit of that replicate, and a data set that is not drawn is left out. Each output mapping is drawn on its own. Data weights are kept: a data set with a data weight of 3 enters the draw as three copies, so on average it keeps its share in the fit.

### Aggregated Data

A data set with a `yErrorType` and error values reports a mean and an SD per time point, or a geometric mean and a geometric SD, instead of individual subjects. Such a data set cannot be resampled by drawing subjects. Instead, each replicate draws a new mean at every time point around the reported one. The new means follow a lognormal distribution, so they stay positive.

The spread of the new means is the one that a mean of `n` subjects has. For an arithmetic mean, this is the standard error $\mathrm{SD}/\sqrt{n}$. For a geometric mean, the spread applies on the log scale and is $\log(\mathrm{GSD})/\sqrt{n}$.

The number of subjects `n` is not stored in the data set, so it has to be set on the output mapping before the bootstrap runs. One number applies to all data sets of the mapping. When the data sets come from studies of different size, give one number per data set, named by the data set:

```{r}
outputMapping$setSubjectCount(12)
outputMapping$setSubjectCount(c("StudyA" = 8, "StudyB" = 20))
```

Only points with a positive mean and an SD above 0, or a GSD above 1, are redrawn. An aggregated data set with at least one such point needs a subject count, otherwise the bootstrap stops with an error before the first replicate.

### Limits for Aggregated Data

In a study, the means at different time points are correlated, because the same subjects contribute to all of them. A mean and an SD do not carry this information, so the bootstrap draws each time point independently. When the differences between subjects mostly raise or lower the whole curve, the intervals tend to be too narrow for parameters that set the level of the curve, such as clearance or bioavailability, and too wide for parameters that set its shape, such as the absorption rate.

The part of the interval width that comes from the redrawn means scales roughly with $1/\sqrt{n}$. When the number of subjects is uncertain, repeat the estimation with a few plausible values and check whether the conclusions change.

## Reading CI Results

The printout of a `PIResult` object shows the main outcomes of a parameter identification run, including parameter estimates, standard deviations, coefficients of variation, and confidence intervals (if available).

For programmatic access, the results can be exported as a data frame or as a list. The data frame has one row per parameter, with the estimate, its standard deviation and coefficient of variation, the confidence bounds and `ciType`, which only `bootstrap` sets. The list holds all details of the run, including the cost.

```{r}
resultTable <- piResult$toDataFrame()
resultList <- piResult$toList()
```

The list also contains a `ciDetails` entry with method-specific information:

- `hessian`: Hessian matrix, covariance matrix, eigenvalues, and correlation matrix
- `PL`: the profile of each parameter, with the parameter value and the cost at each step
- `bootstrap`: the parameter estimates of all replicates, their correlation matrix, and the subject counts used for aggregated data

With `bootstrap`, the parameter estimate can fall outside the interval of the replicates. This happens with strongly skewed distributions, but also when replicates reach a different optimum than the fit or stop at a parameter bound, so inspect the replicates in `ciDetails`. The package then sets the conflicting bound to `NA` and `ciType` to `"one-sided"`. The remaining bound is the same quantile as in the two-sided interval, so it is not a one-sided interval at the chosen confidence level. A regular interval has the `ciType` `"two-sided"`.

## Practical Tips

- Start with the `hessian` method as it is the default and runs quickly. If confidence intervals appear implausible (very wide, a bound below zero or outside the parameter bounds, or `NA`), repeat the analysis with `bootstrap`. Bootstrap needs several individual data sets per output mapping or aggregated data with a subject count. With a single individual data set, every replicate fits the same data and the interval does not reflect the uncertainty.

- When CI calculation fails, check parameter bounds, scaling (`lin` or `log`), and residual weighting. Poorly chosen settings in these areas often prevent reliable CI estimation.

- For `bootstrap`, begin with a small number of resamples (for example 100–200) to test the setup, then increase as needed. Always set a `seed` if reproducible results are required.
